# Carpet roll calculator

> Estimate full-width broadloom carpet strips and total linear roll length for a rectangular room—showing the exact difference between floor area and purchased roll area.

## Calculator
- [Open the calculator](https://measurepuff.com/): US bedroom: a 15 × 12 ft room (180 sq ft) on a 12 ft roll with 3 in end trim needs 15.50 linear ft (186 sq ft / 20.7 sq yd). Metric: a 5 × 4 m room on a 4 m roll with 0.10 m end trim needs 1 strip: 5.20 linear meters (20.80 m² purchased).

## Guide
- [How to work out how much carpet you need](https://measurepuff.com/guide/): step-by-step measuring, common mistakes, and ordering checklist.

## Formula and method
Strips = ceiling(room width / roll width); Cut length per strip = room length + 2 × end trim; Linear roll length = strips × cut length; Purchased area = linear length × roll width.

Divide room width by the fixed carpet roll width and round up to whole strips. Add trimming allowance at both ends of each strip, then multiply by strip count for total linear length. When changing the common lay direction is allowed, both room orientations are compared and the shorter linear roll length is selected.

## Limits
All strips share one pile direction—never rotate an off-cut 90 degrees to patch a side strip. Stairs, L-shaped rooms, bay windows, patterned repeats, doorway seams, and supplier cut increments require an installer cutting plan.

## Standard broadloom carpet roll widths and planning tips

Stepping up from a 12 ft to a 15 ft roll (or 4 m to 5 m) can remove a seam entirely and sometimes reduce total purchased area.

| Market | Standard roll width | Area per linear unit | Seam & layout notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| US standard broadloom | 12 ft (3.66 m) | 12 sq ft / linear ft (1.33 sq yd / ft) | Most widely stocked residential width |
| US wide broadloom | 15 ft (4.57 m) | 15 sq ft / linear ft (1.67 sq yd / ft) | Eliminates seams in 13–15 ft wide rooms |
| UK / European standard | 4 m (13.12 ft) | 4 m² per linear meter | Standard European residential roll |
| UK / European wide | 5 m (16.40 ft) | 5 m² per linear meter | Avoids joins in wider living rooms |
| End trim allowance | 3–4 in (8–10 cm) / end | Add 6–8 in per strip length | Allows power-stretching and baseboard tuck |

## Step by step
1. Measure the longest length and widest width of the room, measuring into doorways, alcoves, closets, and bay windows.
2. Confirm the roll width stocked for your chosen carpet—commonly 12 ft (or 15 ft) in the US and 4 m (or 5 m) in the UK and Europe.
3. Add a trimming allowance of about 3 to 4 in (8 to 10 cm) at each end of every strip for stretching and tucking against baseboards.
4. Check whether changing the lay direction reduces strip count or linear length, keeping in mind that all pieces must keep pile running the same way.

## Common mistakes
- Multiplying room length × width and ordering that square footage. A 14 × 14 ft room needs two 12-ft-wide strips unless a 15-ft roll is used.
- Turning an off-cut 90 degrees to fill a side strip. Carpet pile reflects light differently across angles and looks like a mismatched color patch.
- Placing seams right across doorways or main traffic paths where foot traffic frays joins fastest.
- Forgetting stairs, landings, or pattern repeats on striped and plaid carpets.

## Worked examples
### Example 1
Metric: a 5 × 4 m room on a 4 m roll with 0.10 m end trim needs 1 strip: 5.20 linear meters (20.80 m² purchased).

### Example 2
US bedroom: a 15 × 12 ft room (180 sq ft) on a 12 ft roll with 3 in end trim needs 15.50 linear ft (186 sq ft / 20.7 sq yd).

### Example 3
Two-strip example: a 5 × 5 m room from a 4 m roll needs two 5 m strips (10 linear m / 40 m² purchased) despite 25 m² floor area.
